title: Contributing to tidylearn
text: tidylearn follows standard R package convention described R Packages (2e), §21.2: Released versions CRAN use three components: X.Y.Z (e.g. 0.5.0). Development versions — state package CRAN releases — append fourth component .9000 last released version. CRAN 0.5.0, main branch reads Version: 0.5.0.9000 entire time working toward next release. .9000 suffix signal says “dev build, CRAN release.” maintainer ready submit next release CRAN, version bumped 0.6.0 (dropping .9000), submitted, immediately bumped back 0.6.0.9000 main next dev cycle. ’ll sometimes see .9001, .9002, etc. used mark meaningful dev milestones, .9000 alone default fine ordinary PRs.

title: Contributing to tidylearn
text: Follow surrounding code. package leans tidyverse conventions: snake_case function variable names. exception name mirrors argument wrapped package — e.g. n.trees (gbm), minPts (dbscan), B (cluster::clusGap) — keeps package’s spelling interface stays familiar. .lintr allows dotted.case camelCase reason; .lintr parsed strict DCF carry comment, hence note. <- (=) assignment. Exported functions need roxygen documentation @param, @return, @examples, @export. lintr::lint_package() report issues. Install package first (R CMD INSTALL . devtools::install()) object_usage_linter can resolve namespace — otherwise reports spurious “visible global function definition” lints package’s internal functions.

text: Real-world data often split across multiple files. tidylearn handles three common patterns.

title: Data Ingestion with tidylearn
text: Pass character vector tl_read() — file read row-bound, source_file column tracking origin:
code: dir <- tempdir() write.csv(iris[1:50, ], file.path(dir, "batch1.csv"), row.names = FALSE) write.csv(iris[51:100, ], file.path(dir, "batch2.csv"), row.names = FALSE)  paths <- file.path(dir, c("batch1.csv", "batch2.csv")) combined <- tl_read(paths, .quiet = TRUE) table(combined$source_file) #>  #> batch1.csv batch2.csv  #>         50         50

title: Data Ingestion with tidylearn
text: Point tl_read_dir() directory. Filter format, regex pattern, scan recursively: Passing directory path directly tl_read() works :
code: dir <- tempfile(pattern = "tl_vignette_") dir.create(dir) write.csv(iris[1:50, ], file.path(dir, "jan.csv"), row.names = FALSE) write.csv(iris[51:100, ], file.path(dir, "feb.csv"), row.names = FALSE) write.csv(iris[101:150, ], file.path(dir, "mar.csv"), row.names = FALSE)  # Read all CSVs from the directory all_data <- tl_read_dir(dir, format = "csv", .quiet = TRUE) nrow(all_data) #> [1] 150 table(all_data$source_file) #>  #> feb.csv jan.csv mar.csv  #>      50      50      50 # Filter with a regex pattern subset <- tl_read_dir(dir, pattern = "^(jan|feb)", .quiet = TRUE) nrow(subset) #> [1] 100 data <- tl_read("data/monthly_exports/")

title: Data Ingestion with tidylearn
text: tl_read_zip() extracts archive, auto-detects file format, reads contents. Select specific file let discover data files automatically: Zip files also auto-detected tl_read():
code: # Create an example zip dir <- tempfile(pattern = "tl_zip_src_") dir.create(dir) write.csv(iris, file.path(dir, "iris.csv"), row.names = FALSE) zip_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip") # -j stores the file without its directory path, so no setwd() is needed utils::zip(zip_path, file.path(dir, "iris.csv"), flags = "-j9X")  zip_data <- tl_read_zip(zip_path, .quiet = TRUE) nrow(zip_data) #> [1] 150 attr(zip_data, "tl_format") #> [1] "zip+csv" data <- tl_read("download.zip") data <- tl_read("download.zip", file = "train.csv")

text: Every reader returns tidylearn_data object — tibble subclass three metadata attributes: tidylearn_data inherits tbl_df, dplyr verbs, ggplot2, tidylearn functions work transparently:
code: tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv") write.csv(mtcars, tmp, row.names = FALSE) data <- tl_read(tmp, .quiet = TRUE)  # Check metadata attr(data, "tl_format") #> [1] "csv"  # Works with dplyr data |>   filter(mpg > 20) |>   select(mpg, wt, hp) |>   head(3) #> -- tidylearn data --------- #> Source: /tmp/Rtmp8JEUmW/file2d2744c0243a.csv  #> Format: csv  #> Read at: 2026-10-08 18:00:16  #>  #> # A tibble: 3 × 3 #>     mpg    wt    hp #>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1  21    2.62   110 #> 2  21    2.88   110 #> 3  22.8  2.32    93

title: Data Ingestion with tidylearn
text: Combining tl_read() rest tidylearn gives complete workflow raw data published results:
code: # 1. Ingest tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv") write.csv(iris, tmp, row.names = FALSE) data <- tl_read(tmp, .quiet = TRUE)  # CSV files lose factor information, so convert character columns as needed data <- data |> mutate(Species = as.factor(Species))  # 2. Split split <- tl_split(data, prop = 0.7, stratify = "Species", seed = 42)  # 3. Model model <- tl_model(split$train, Species ~ ., method = "forest")  # 4. Evaluate eval_result <- tl_evaluate(model, new_data = split$test) eval_result #> # A tibble: 1 × 2 #>   metric   value #>   <chr>    <dbl> #> 1 accuracy 0.956

title: Diagnostics
text: model fits model use. functions answer four questions: assumptions hold? tl_check_assumptions() observations drove fit? tl_influence_measures(), tl_detect_outliers() difference two models real? tl_compare_cv(), tl_test_model_difference() interactions modelled? tl_test_interactions(), tl_interaction_effects() tl_explore() runs unsupervised sweep dataset model . use linear model throughout, assumption checking teeth.
code: model <- tl_model(mtcars, mpg ~ wt + hp + disp, method = "linear")

title: Diagnostics
text: tl_check_assumptions() runs six checks returns verdict . entry carries test run, verdict, . Nothing pass/fail gate — recommendation prompt, instruction. compact table every check: disp correlating wt hp drives VIF , kind thing invisible coefficient table.
code: assumptions <- tl_check_assumptions(model, verbose = FALSE) names(assumptions) #> [1] "linearity"         "independence"      "homoscedasticity"  #> [4] "normality"         "multicollinearity" "outliers"          #> [7] "overall" assumptions$overall #> $status #> [1] "5 assumption(s) appear to be violated. See details." #>  #> $n_checked #> [1] 6 #>  #> $n_violated #> [1] 5 #>  #> $n_satisfied #> [1] 1 assumptions$normality #> $assumption #> [1] "Normality of Residuals" #>  #> $check #> [1] FALSE #>  #> $details #> [1] "Shapiro-Wilk test p-value: 0.033" #>  #> $recommendation #> [1] "Residuals may not be normally distributed. Consider transformations or robust regression." assumptions$multicollinearity #> $assumption #> [1] "No Multicollinearity" #>  #> $check #> [1] FALSE #>  #> $details #> [1] "Maximum VIF: 7.3245" #>  #> $recommendation #> [1] "Multicollinearity detected. Consider removing or combining highly correlated predictors." checks <- c("linearity", "independence", "homoscedasticity",             "normality", "multicollinearity", "outliers")  data.frame(   assumption = vapply(checks, function(x) assumptions[[x]]$assumption,                       character(1)),   holds = vapply(checks, function(x) isTRUE(assumptions[[x]]$check),                  logical(1)),   detail = vapply(checks, function(x) assumptions[[x]]$details, character(1)),   row.names = NULL ) #>                assumption holds #> 1               Linearity FALSE #> 2            Independence FALSE #> 3        Homoscedasticity  TRUE #> 4  Normality of Residuals FALSE #> 5    No Multicollinearity FALSE #> 6 No Influential Outliers FALSE #>                                                                detail #> 1 RESET-style test on powers of the fitted values: p-value = 0.001944 #> 2                                     Durbin-Watson statistic: 1.3673 #> 3                                  Breusch-Pagan test p-value: 0.8143 #> 4                                    Shapiro-Wilk test p-value: 0.033 #> 5                                                 Maximum VIF: 7.3245 #> 6                                 4 influential observations detected

Set plot = TRUE get ggplot2 object back $plot.

code: simple <- tl_model(mtcars, mpg ~ wt, method = "linear") full <- tl_model(mtcars, mpg ~ wt + hp + disp, method = "linear") tree <- tl_model(mtcars, mpg ~ wt + hp + disp, method = "tree")  cv <- tl_compare_cv(   mtcars,   models = list(simple = simple, full = full, tree = tree),   folds = 5,   metrics = c("rmse", "rsq") )  names(cv) #> [1] "fold_metrics" "summary" cv$summary #> # A tibble: 6 × 6 #>   model  metric mean_value sd_value min_value max_value #>   <chr>  <chr>       <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl> #> 1 full   rmse      2.68       1.33      1.43      4.84  #> 2 full   rsq       0.739      0.164     0.586     0.920 #> 3 simple rmse      2.95       1.42      1.79      5.32  #> 4 simple rsq       0.689      0.184     0.517     0.907 #> 5 tree   rmse      5.03       0.878     3.70      5.76  #> 6 tree   rsq       0.00252    0.634    -0.902     0.505 head(cv$fold_metrics) #> # A tibble: 6 × 4 #>   metric value  fold model  #>   <chr>  <dbl> <int> <chr>  #> 1 rmse   1.79      1 simple #> 2 rsq    0.859     1 simple #> 3 rmse   2.85      2 simple #> 4 rsq    0.638     2 simple #> 5 rmse   2.88      3 simple #> 6 rsq    0.524     3 simple

title: Diagnostics
text: tl_test_model_difference() compares model baseline using per-fold scores. five folds little power, treat non-significant result “folds separate models” rather evidence equivalent. test = "wilcox" runs signed-rank test instead, drops normality assumption needs least six folds return p-value 0.05. five pairs fold scores smallest two-sided p-value can give 0.0625, one model wins every fold:
code: tl_test_model_difference(   cv,   baseline_model = "simple",   metric = "rmse",   test = "t.test" ) #>   metric model baseline  mean_diff    p_value      p_adj #> 1   rmse  full   simple -0.2650263 0.51406818 0.51406818 #> 2   rmse  tree   simple  2.0845970 0.04201286 0.08402572 tl_test_model_difference(   cv,   baseline_model = "simple",   metric = "rmse",   test = "wilcox" ) #>   metric model baseline  mean_diff p_value  p_adj #> 1   rmse  full   simple -0.2650263  0.4375 0.4375 #> 2   rmse  tree   simple  2.0845970  0.0625 0.1250

title: Diagnostics
text: tl_test_interactions() fits candidate interaction reports whether earns degrees freedom. delta_r2 useful column: p-value tells term detectable, delta_r2 tells whether worth carrying. Restrict search numeric_only, categorical_only mixed_only, name single pair var1 var2.
code: interactions <- tl_test_interactions(   mtcars, mpg ~ wt + hp + disp,   all_pairs = TRUE )  interactions #>   var1 var2     p_value significant   delta_r2 f_statistic #> 1   wt   hp 0.000950209        TRUE 0.05845233    13.75810 #> 3   hp disp 0.001238835        TRUE 0.05631176    13.01147 #> 2   wt disp 0.003839687        TRUE 0.04681464    10.00398

title: Diagnostics
text: term model, tl_interaction_effects() says different levels moderator. slope mpg wt weakens hp rises — extra weight costs less fuel economy high-powered car, already little lose. slope_se describes straight line fitted prediction grid rather sampling uncertainty marginal effect — linear model grid exactly linear, near zero construction. Use tl_coefficients() inference interaction coefficient . tl_auto_interactions() search refit one step, returning model surviving interactions already formula:
code: model_int <- tl_model(mtcars, mpg ~ wt * hp, method = "linear") effects <- tl_interaction_effects(model_int, var = "wt", by_var = "hp")  effects$slopes #>      by_value by_label     slope     slope_se #> Q0       52.0       Q0 -6.768521 3.505829e-16 #> Q25      96.5      Q25 -5.529278 4.039654e-16 #> Q50     123.0      Q50 -4.791302 3.746703e-16 #> Q75     180.0      Q75 -3.203958 4.635819e-16 #> Q100    335.0     Q100  1.112505 2.313524e-16 tl_coefficients(model_int, conf_int = TRUE) #> # A tibble: 4 × 7 #>   term        estimate std_error conf_low conf_high statistic  p_value #>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl> #> 1 (Intercept)  49.8      3.61     42.4      57.2        13.8  5.01e-14 #> 2 wt           -8.22     1.27    -10.8      -5.62       -6.47 5.20e- 7 #> 3 hp           -0.120    0.0247   -0.171    -0.0695     -4.86 4.04e- 5 #> 4 wt:hp         0.0278   0.00742   0.0126    0.0430      3.75 8.11e- 4 auto <- tl_auto_interactions(mtcars, mpg ~ wt + hp + disp) auto$spec$formula #> mpg ~ wt + hp + disp + wt:hp + hp:disp + wt:disp

title: Getting Started with tidylearn
text: Logistic regression handles two-class problems, take binary subset iris . three classes use "tree", "forest", "svm" "nn". Predictions come back tibble .pred column. .pred contains depends type: "class" gives predicted label, "prob" gives one column per class. Note default type = "response" means different things across methods — probabilities logistic regression, class labels trees forests. Ask type = "class" explicitly want labels, let tl_evaluate() handle :
code: # versicolor and virginica overlap, so this is a real classification # problem -- setosa is linearly separable from the other two, which makes # logistic regression fail to converge iris_binary <- iris |>   filter(Species %in% c("versicolor", "virginica")) |>   mutate(Species = droplevels(Species))  model_logistic <- tl_model(iris_binary, Species ~ ., method = "logistic") print(model_logistic) #> tidylearn Model #> =============== #> Paradigm: supervised  #> Method: logistic  #> Task: Classification  #> Formula: Species ~ .  #>  #> Training observations: 100 # Predicted class labels predictions <- predict(model_logistic, type = "class") head(predictions) #> # A tibble: 6 × 1 #>   .pred      #>   <fct>      #> 1 versicolor #> 2 versicolor #> 3 versicolor #> 4 versicolor #> 5 versicolor #> 6 versicolor # Class probabilities head(predict(model_logistic, type = "prob")) #> # A tibble: 6 × 2 #>   versicolor virginica #>        <dbl>     <dbl> #> 1      1.000 0.0000117 #> 2      1.000 0.0000486 #> 3      0.999 0.00120   #> 4      1.000 0.0000422 #> 5      0.999 0.00141   #> 6      1.000 0.000102 tl_evaluate(model_logistic, metrics = c("accuracy", "f1")) #> # A tibble: 2 × 2 #>   metric   value #>   <chr>    <dbl> #> 1 accuracy  0.98 #> 2 f1        0.98

Use tl_evaluate() rather than comparing $.pred by # hand: what $.pred holds depends on the method and prediction type. tl_evaluate(model_reduced) #> # A tibble: 1 × 2 #>   metric   value #>   <chr>    <dbl> #> 1 accuracy     1

code:
# Split data for fair comparison split <- tl_split(iris, prop = 0.7, stratify = "Species", seed = 123)  # Model with original features model_original <- tl_model(split$train, Species ~ ., method = "forest") eval_original <- tl_evaluate(model_original, new_data = split$test)  # Model with PCA features reduced_train <- tl_reduce_dimensions(split$train,                                       response = "Species",                                       method = "pca",                                       n_components = 3)  model_pca <- tl_model(reduced_train$data, Species ~ ., method = "forest")  # The test set must be projected through the PCA fitted on the training # data -- refitting PCA on the test set would leak information test_transformed <- predict(   reduced_train$reduction_model,   new_data = split$test |> select(-Species) ) test_transformed$Species <- split$test$Species  eval_pca <- tl_evaluate(model_pca, new_data = test_transformed)  # Compare results acc <- function(x) round(x$value[x$metric == "accuracy"] * 100, 1) n_original <- ncol(split$train) - 1 n_reduced <- sum(grepl("^PC", names(reduced_train$data))) cat("Original features:", n_original, "->", acc(eval_original), "%
") #> Original features: 4 -> 93.3 % cat("PCA features:", n_reduced, "->", acc(eval_pca), "%
") #> PCA features: 3 -> 91.1 % cat("Feature reduction:",     round((1 - n_reduced / n_original) * 100, 1), "%
") #> Feature reduction: 25 %

code: # Compare models with and without cluster features split_comp <- tl_split(iris, prop = 0.7, stratify = "Species", seed = 42)  # Without cluster features model_no_cluster <- tl_model(split_comp$train, Species ~ ., method = "forest") preds_no_cluster <- predict(model_no_cluster, new_data = split_comp$test) acc_no_cluster <- mean(preds_no_cluster$.pred == split_comp$test$Species)  # With cluster features train_clustered <- tl_add_cluster_features(split_comp$train,                                            response = "Species",                                            method = "kmeans",                                            k = 3) model_with_cluster <- tl_model(train_clustered, Species ~ ., method = "forest")  # Need to get cluster model for test data cluster_model <- attr(train_clustered, "cluster_model") test_clusters <- predict(cluster_model, new_data = split_comp$test[, -5]) test_clustered <- split_comp$test test_clustered$cluster_kmeans <- as.factor(test_clusters$cluster)  preds_with_cluster <- predict(model_with_cluster, new_data = test_clustered) acc_with_cluster <- mean(preds_with_cluster$.pred == split_comp$test$Species)  cat("Without cluster features:", round(acc_no_cluster * 100, 1), "%\n") #> Without cluster features: 95.6 % cat("With cluster features:", round(acc_with_cluster * 100, 1), "%\n") #> With cluster features: 93.3 %

code: # Use only 10% of labels set.seed(123) labeled_indices <- sample(nrow(iris), size = 15)  # 15 of 150 labelled  # supervised_method defaults to "tree". Named here because a forest is # the better fit for propagated labels: the propagation step introduces # noise, and averaging over trees absorbs more of it than one tree does. model_semi <- tl_semisupervised(iris, Species ~ .,                                 labeled_indices = labeled_indices,                                 cluster_method = "kmeans",                                 supervised_method = "forest")  print(model_semi) #> tidylearn Model #> =============== #> Paradigm: supervised  #> Method: forest  #> Task: Classification  #> Formula: Species ~ .  #>  #> Training observations: 150 # Check how labels were propagated label_mapping <- model_semi$semisupervised_info$label_mapping print(label_mapping) #> # A tibble: 3 × 2 #>   cluster cluster_label #>     <int> <chr>         #> 1       1 virginica     #> 2       2 versicolor    #> 3       3 setosa # Evaluate against the true labels preds_semi <- predict(model_semi, new_data = iris, type = "class") accuracy_semi <- mean(preds_semi$.pred == iris$Species)  cat("Accuracy with only", length(labeled_indices), "labels:",     round(accuracy_semi * 100, 1), "%\n") #> Accuracy with only 15 labels: 90 % labeled_pct <- round(   length(labeled_indices) / nrow(iris) * 100, 1 ) cat("Proportion of data labeled:", labeled_pct, "%\n") #> Proportion of data labeled: 10 %

title: Integration Workflows: Combining Supervised and Unsupervised Learning
text: Combining multiple integration techniques:
code: # Step 1: Split data workflow_split <- tl_split(iris, prop = 0.7, stratify = "Species", seed = 42)  # Step 2: Reduce dimensions workflow_reduced <- tl_reduce_dimensions(workflow_split$train,                                          response = "Species",                                          method = "pca",                                          n_components = 3)  # Step 3: Add cluster features to reduced data workflow_clustered <- tl_add_cluster_features(workflow_reduced$data,                                               response = "Species",                                               method = "kmeans",                                               k = 3)  # Step 4: Train final model workflow_model <- tl_model(workflow_clustered, Species ~ ., method = "forest")  print(workflow_model) #> tidylearn Model #> =============== #> Paradigm: supervised  #> Method: forest  #> Task: Classification  #> Formula: Species ~ .  #>  #> Training observations: 105 # Transform test data through same pipeline # 1. Apply PCA transformation test_pca <- predict(workflow_reduced$reduction_model,                     new_data = workflow_split$test[, -5]) test_pca$Species <- workflow_split$test$Species  # 2. Get cluster assignments. The cluster model was fitted on the PC # columns; predict() matches new_data to those columns by name and # errors on a mismatch rather than assigning against the wrong ones. cluster_model_wf <- attr(workflow_clustered, "cluster_model") test_clusters_wf <- predict(cluster_model_wf, new_data = test_pca) test_pca$cluster_kmeans <- as.factor(test_clusters_wf$cluster)  # 3. Predict workflow_preds <- predict(workflow_model, new_data = test_pca) workflow_accuracy <- mean(workflow_preds$.pred == workflow_split$test$Species)  cat("Complete Workflow Accuracy:", round(workflow_accuracy * 100, 1), "%\n") #> Complete Workflow Accuracy: 91.1 %

title: Integration Workflows: Combining Supervised and Unsupervised Learning
code: # Simulate credit data set.seed(42) n <- 500 credit_data <- data.frame(   age = rnorm(n, 40, 12),   income = rnorm(n, 50000, 20000),   debt_ratio = runif(n, 0, 0.5),   credit_score = rnorm(n, 700, 100),   years_employed = rpois(n, 5) )  # Create target variable (default risk) credit_data$default <- factor(   ifelse(     credit_data$debt_ratio > 0.4 & credit_data$credit_score < 650,     "Yes", "No"   ) )  # Split data credit_split <- tl_split(   credit_data, prop = 0.7, stratify = "default", seed = 123 ) # Strategy 1: Add customer segments as features credit_clustered <- tl_add_cluster_features(credit_split$train,                                             response = "default",                                             method = "kmeans",                                             k = 4)  model_credit <- tl_model(credit_clustered, default ~ ., method = "forest")  # Transform test data cluster_model_credit <- attr(credit_clustered, "cluster_model") test_clusters_credit <- predict(cluster_model_credit,                                 new_data = credit_split$test[, -6]) test_credit <- credit_split$test test_credit$cluster_kmeans <- as.factor(test_clusters_credit$cluster)  preds_credit <- predict(model_credit, new_data = test_credit) accuracy_credit <- mean(preds_credit$.pred == credit_split$test$default)  cat("Credit Risk Model Accuracy:", round(accuracy_credit * 100, 1), "%\n") #> Credit Risk Model Accuracy: 100 %

title: Supervised Learning with tidylearn
text: Let’s create binary classification problem iris dataset:
code: # Create binary classification dataset. setosa is linearly separable from # the other two species, and logistic regression has no finite maximum # likelihood estimate on separable data -- glm() fits, warns that the # algorithm did not converge, and returns coefficients that diverged. # versicolor and virginica overlap, so this is a real classification # problem. Even here, a 70% split of 100 rows is separable at some seeds; # this one is not. iris_binary <- iris |>   filter(Species %in% c("versicolor", "virginica")) |>   mutate(Species = droplevels(Species))  # Split data split <- tl_split(iris_binary, prop = 0.7, stratify = "Species", seed = 42)

what: Replaying Preprocessing on the Test Set
title: Supervised Learning with tidylearn
text: model trained scaled features expects scaled inputs prediction time. tl_prepare_data() keeps parameters learned, transformation can replayed test set — applying training centre scale, never recomputing test data: Skipping step predicting raw test data common quiet mistake — model still returns predictions, just wrong. multi-step preprocessing, tl_pipeline() handles bookkeeping : tl_predict_pipeline() replays training preprocessing automatically.
code: # Complete workflow example final_split <- tl_split(iris, prop = 0.7, stratify = "Species", seed = 42)  final_prep <- tl_prepare_data(   final_split$train, Species ~ .,   scale_method = "standardize" ) #> Scaling numeric features using method: standardize final_model <- tl_model(final_prep$data, Species ~ ., method = "forest") scaling <- final_prep$preprocessing_steps$scaling$scaling_params  final_test <- final_split$test for (col in names(scaling)) {   final_test[[col]] <-     (final_test[[col]] - scaling[[col]]$mean) / scaling[[col]]$sd }  final_preds <- predict(final_model, new_data = final_test) accuracy <- mean(final_preds$.pred == final_split$test$Species) cat("Test Accuracy:", round(accuracy * 100, 1), "%\n") #> Test Accuracy: 95.6 %

title: Tuning and Pipelines
text: tl_model() fits one model hyperparameters name. Two families build : Tuning searches space hyperparameters returns model fitted winner. tl_tune_grid() walks every combination; tl_tune_random() samples ranges. Pipelines bundle preprocessing, set models, evaluation scheme one object can run, save, reload, predict . two compose: tune find settings, put winning settings pipeline whole recipe reproducible.

title: Tuning and Pipelines
text: tl_tune_grid() takes named list candidate values, one entry per hyperparameter, cross-validates every combination. comes back ordinary tidylearn model, already fitted winning settings, everything normally model still works: search attached "tuning_results" attribute: winning values reach underlying fit, just report:
code: tuned_tree <- tl_tune_grid(   iris, Species ~ .,   method = "tree",   param_grid = list(cp = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1), minsplit = c(5, 20)),   folds = 3,   verbose = FALSE ) print(tuned_tree) #> tidylearn Model #> =============== #> Paradigm: supervised  #> Method: tree  #> Task: Classification  #> Formula: Species ~ .  #>  #> Training observations: 150 tuning <- attr(tuned_tree, "tuning_results") names(tuning) #> [1] "param_grid"  "results"     "best_params" "best_metric" "metric"      #> [6] "maximize" tuning$results #>   mean_metric n_folds_ok    cp minsplit #> 1   0.9666667          3 0.001        5 #> 2   0.9466667          3 0.001       20 #> 3   0.9666667          3 0.010        5 #> 4   0.9466667          3 0.010       20 #> 5   0.9466667          3 0.100        5 #> 6   0.9466667          3 0.100       20 # The settings that won, and the score they won with tuning$best_params #> $cp #> [1] 0.001 #>  #> $minsplit #> [1] 5 tuning$best_metric #> [1] 0.9666667 tuned_tree$fit$control$cp #> [1] 0.001

title: Tuning and Pipelines
text: pipeline records preprocessing, models fit, evaluate . Building work; tl_run_pipeline() . Anything leave preprocessing evaluation takes default, partial list fine. unrecognised name error rather step quietly nothing.
code: split <- tl_split(iris, prop = 0.7, stratify = "Species", seed = 42)  pipe <- tl_pipeline(   split$train, Species ~ .,   preprocessing = list(standardize = TRUE),   models = list(     tree = list(method = "tree"),     forest = list(method = "forest", ntree = 300)   ),   evaluation = list(     validation = "cv",     cv_folds = 3,     metrics = c("accuracy", "f1"),     best_metric = "accuracy"   ) )  print(pipe) #> Tidylearn Pipeline #> ================= #> Formula: Species ~ .  #> Data: 105 observations, 5 variables #> Preprocessing: impute_missing, standardize, dummy_encode  #> Models: tree, forest  #> Evaluation:  cv (3 folds) #> Metrics: accuracy, f1  #> Best metric: accuracy tl_pipeline(split$train, Species ~ .,             preprocessing = list(scale_method = "standardize")) #> Error: #> ! Unknown preprocessing step(s): scale_method. Available steps: impute_missing, standardize, dummy_encode.

code: pam_result <- tidy_pam(iris[, 1:4], k = 3) pam_result$medoids #> # A tibble: 3 × 6 #>   cluster medoid_index Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width #>     <int>        <int>        <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> #> 1       1            8          5           3.4          1.5         0.2 #> 2       2           79          6           2.9          4.5         1.5 #> 3       3          113          6.8         3            5.5         2.1 pam_result$silhouette_avg #> [1] 0.552819 table(Cluster = augment_pam(pam_result, iris)$cluster, Species = iris$Species) #>        Species #> Cluster setosa versicolor virginica #>       1     50          0         0 #>       2      0         48        14 #>       3      0          2        36 large_data <- iris[rep(seq_len(nrow(iris)), 10), 1:4] clara_result <- tidy_clara(large_data, k = 3, samples = 5)  table(clara_result$clusters$cluster) #>  #>   1   2   3  #> 500 380 620

title: Unsupervised Learning with tidylearn
text: tidy_hclust() builds tree; cutting separate decision.  optimal_hclust_k() scores cut heights way optimal_clusters() scores k: Linkage matters people expect. "average", "complete", "single" "ward.D2" can produce different trees distances: Single linkage chains: largest cluster takes 98 150 rows, versicolor nearly virginica, leaves two rows cluster . property linkage, finding irises.
code: hc <- tidy_hclust(iris[, 1:4], method = "average") plot_dendrogram(hc, k = 3) optimal_hclust_k(hc, method = "silhouette", max_k = 8)$optimal_k #> [1] 2 cuts <- tidy_cutree(hc, k = 3) head(cuts, 3) #> # A tibble: 3 × 2 #>   .obs_id cluster #>   <chr>     <int> #> 1 1             1 #> 2 2             1 #> 3 3             1 hc_data <- augment_hclust(hc, iris, k = 3) table(Cluster = hc_data$cluster, Species = hc_data$Species) #>        Species #> Cluster setosa versicolor virginica #>       1     50          0         0 #>       2      0         50        14 #>       3      0          0        36 linkages <- c("single", "average", "complete", "ward.D2")  sapply(linkages, function(m) {   cl <- tidy_cutree(tidy_hclust(iris[, 1:4], method = m), k = 3)$cluster   max(table(cl)) }) #>   single  average complete  ward.D2  #>       98       64       72       64

title: Unsupervised Learning with tidylearn
text: DBSCAN finds arbitrarily shaped clusters labels sparse points noise. needs eps (neighbourhood radius) minPts. Rather guessing, suggest_eps() reads k-nearest-neighbour distance curve, k = minPts - 1 core point’s minPts includes point .  elbow curve points stop close neighbours, radius want. Cluster 0 noise, cluster. explore_dbscan_params() sweeps two parameters together, informative tuning either alone: Read prop_noise alongside n_clusters: setting finds many clusters discarding third data found structure.
code: eps_suggestion <- suggest_eps(iris[, 1:4], minPts = 5) eps_suggestion$eps #> [1] 0.7179749 plot_knn_dist(iris[, 1:4], k = 4) db <- tidy_dbscan(iris[, 1:4], eps = eps_suggestion$eps, minPts = 5)  c(clusters = db$n_clusters, noise = db$n_noise) #> clusters    noise  #>        2        3 db_data <- augment_dbscan(db, iris) table(Cluster = db_data$cluster, Species = db_data$Species) #>        Species #> Cluster setosa versicolor virginica #>       0      0          0         3 #>       1     50          0         0 #>       2      0         50        47 explore_dbscan_params(   iris[, 1:4],   eps_values = c(0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0),   minPts_values = c(4, 5, 10) ) #> # A tibble: 12 × 5 #>      eps minPts n_clusters n_noise prop_noise #>    <dbl>  <dbl>      <int>   <int>      <dbl> #>  1   0.4      4          4      25     0.167  #>  2   0.6      4          3       5     0.0333 #>  3   0.8      4          2       2     0.0133 #>  4   1        4          2       0     0      #>  5   0.4      5          4      32     0.213  #>  6   0.6      5          2       9     0.06   #>  7   0.8      5          2       2     0.0133 #>  8   1        5          2       0     0      #>  9   0.4     10          3      83     0.553  #> 10   0.6     10          2      13     0.0867 #> 11   0.8     10          2       5     0.0333 #> 12   1       10          2       0     0

title: Unsupervised Learning with tidylearn
text: MDS places observations plotted distances reproduce distances original space. Unlike PCA can work distance matrix, including non-Euclidean ones.  method also takes "metric" "nonmetric" (via smacof), "sammon" "kruskal". last two minimise stress function dividing observed distances, need every pairwise distance strictly positive. iris contains one duplicated row, enough stop : Drop duplicates run: Stress number check reading anything non-metric layout: 0.05 picture faithful rendering distances, 0.2 decoration.
code: mds <- tidy_mds(iris[, 1:4], method = "classical", ndim = 2) head(mds$config, 3) #> # A tibble: 3 × 2 #>    Dim1   Dim2 #>   <dbl>  <dbl> #> 1 -2.68  0.319 #> 2 -2.71 -0.177 #> 3 -2.89 -0.145 plot_mds(mds, color_by = iris$Species, label_points = FALSE) tidy_mds(iris[, 1:4], method = "sammon", ndim = 2) #> Error: #> ! method = "sammon" needs every pairwise distance to be positive, but 1 pair(s) of observations are identical: 102 and 143. Drop the duplicates, or use method = "classical", "metric" or "nonmetric", which tolerate them. distinct_iris <- iris[!duplicated(iris[, 1:4]), 1:4] sammon <- tidy_mds(distinct_iris, method = "sammon", ndim = 2) sammon$stress #> [1] 0.004015053

title: Unsupervised Learning with tidylearn
text: Putting pieces order belong:  Silhouette chose 2, table shows means: setosa separated, two species merged. honest reading data metric — third cluster exists botanically well separated four measurements.
code: data_matrix <- standardize_data(iris[, 1:4])  # 1. How many clusters does the data support? choice <- optimal_clusters(data_matrix, max_k = 8) k <- attr(choice$silhouette, "optimal_k") k #> [1] 2 # 2. Cluster at that k final_km <- tidy_kmeans(data_matrix, k = k)  # 3. Score the result before believing it final_sil <- tidy_silhouette(final_km$clusters$cluster, tidy_dist(data_matrix)) final_sil$avg_width #> [1] 0.58175 # 4. Attach the assignment and look at it final_data <- augment_kmeans(final_km, iris) table(Cluster = final_data$cluster, Species = final_data$Species) #>        Species #> Cluster setosa versicolor virginica #>       1      0         50        50 #>       2     50          0         0 plot_clusters(final_data, cluster_col = "cluster",               x_col = "Petal.Length", y_col = "Petal.Width")

title: A unified tidy interface to R's machine learning ecosystem
text: tidylearn provides unified tidyverse-compatible interface R’s machine learning ecosystem. wraps proven packages like glmnet, randomForest, xgboost, e1071, cluster, dbscan - get reliability established implementations convenience consistent, tidy API. tidylearn : Reads data diverse sources (tl_read()) — CSV, Excel, Parquet, JSON, databases, S3, Kaggle, Provides one consistent interface (tl_model()) 20 ML algorithms (13 supervised, 7 unsupervised) Returns tidy tibbles instead varied output formats Offers unified ggplot2-based visualization formatted gt tables Enables pipe-friendly workflows |> Orchestrates complex workflows combining multiple techniques tidylearn : reimplementation ML algorithms (uses established packages hood) replacement underlying packages (can access raw model via model$fit, model$fit$model unsupervised method)

title: A unified tidy interface to R's machine learning ecosystem
text: tl_read() auto-detects format returns tidy tidylearn_data object:
code: library(tidylearn)  # Single files — format auto-detected from extension data <- tl_read("sales.csv") data <- tl_read("results.xlsx", sheet = "Q1") data <- tl_read("experiment.parquet")  # Databases data <- tl_read_sqlite("warehouse.sqlite", "SELECT * FROM sales") data <- tl_read_postgres("localhost", query = "SELECT * FROM customers",                          dbname = "analytics", user = "me")  # Cloud and API sources data <- tl_read_s3("s3://my-bucket/data.csv") data <- tl_read_kaggle("zillow/zecon", file = "Zip_time_series.csv")  # Multi-file reading data <- tl_read(c("jan.csv", "feb.csv", "mar.csv")) data <- tl_read_dir("data/monthly/", format = "csv") data <- tl_read_zip("download.zip")

title: A unified tidy interface to R's machine learning ecosystem
text: single tl_model() function dispatches appropriate underlying package:
code: library(tidylearn)  # Classification -> uses randomForest::randomForest() model <- tl_model(iris, Species ~ ., method = "forest")  # Regression -> uses stats::lm() model <- tl_model(mtcars, mpg ~ wt + hp, method = "linear")  # Regularization -> uses glmnet::glmnet() model <- tl_model(mtcars, mpg ~ ., method = "lasso")  # Clustering -> uses stats::kmeans() model <- tl_model(iris[,1:4], method = "kmeans", k = 3)  # PCA -> uses stats::prcomp() model <- tl_model(iris[,1:4], method = "pca")

title: A unified tidy interface to R's machine learning ecosystem
text: results come back tibbles, ready dplyr ggplot2: classification, .pred holds depends type: "class" gives labels, "prob" gives one column per class. default "response" varies method - probabilities logistic regression, labels trees forests - pass type explicitly, let tl_evaluate() handle .
code: # Predictions come back as a tibble with a .pred column predictions <- predict(model, new_data = test_data)  # Metrics as tibbles - pick the metrics you want metrics <- tl_evaluate(model, test_data) metrics <- tl_evaluate(model, test_data, metrics = c("rmse", "rsq"))  # Coefficients too, with a confidence interval when you ask for one coefs <- tl_coefficients(model) coefs <- tl_coefficients(model, conf_int = TRUE, level = 0.9)  # Easy to pipe model |>   predict(new_data = test_data) |>   bind_cols(test_data) |>   ggplot(aes(x = mpg, y = .pred)) +   geom_point() +   geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0)

text: methods run CPU need thought. two upstream GPU path ("xgboost" "deep"), tl_model() takes compute argument: tl_compute_advisor() estimates runtime, peak memory cost across local CPU, local GPU cloud tiers commit long fit: Estimates order--magnitude. advisor covers 13 supervised methods, treats cloud “fit machine” tier, recommend cloud CPU-method like random forest job RAM-infeasible locally.
code: # Check what this machine can actually do tl_check_gpu()  # Route a fit to the local GPU (falls back to CPU with a warning if # no CUDA-capable backend is detected) model <- tl_model(data, y ~ ., method = "xgboost", compute = "gpu")  # Let tidylearn decide per call model <- tl_model(data, y ~ ., method = "xgboost", compute = "auto") tl_compute_advisor("xgboost", data, y ~ ., hyperparams = list(nrounds = 5000))

title: Predict using a tidylearn model — predict.tidylearn_model
text: object tidylearn model object new_data data frame containing new data. NULL, uses training data. type Type prediction, supervised models : "response" (default), "prob" "class". Note "response" method-dependent – logistic regression returns probabilities, trees forests return class labels – pass "class" explicitly want labels. "prob" "class" need classification model, value error. Ignored unsupervised models, whose output determined method. ... Additional arguments

title: Predict using a tidylearn model — predict.tidylearn_model
text: supervised models, tibble .pred column; type = "prob", one column per class instead. one row per row new_data, order, zero rows zero-row new_data. unsupervised models, method's natural output: .obs_id column, row names data predicted , plus component scores "pca" "mds" (many model keeps), plus cluster column clustering methods. Unsupervised models differ whether can handle new data. "pca" projects "kmeans" assigns nearest centre; "pam", "clara", "dbscan", "mds" "hclust" --sample projection error new_data supplied. hierarchical clustering, cut tree tidy_cutree() instead.

title: tidylearn: A Unified Tidy Interface to R's Machine Learning Ecosystem — tidylearn-package
text: Provides unified tidyverse-compatible interface R's machine learning ecosystem - data ingestion model publishing. tl_read() family reads data files ('CSV', 'Excel', 'Parquet', 'JSON'), databases ('SQLite', 'PostgreSQL', 'MySQL', 'BigQuery'), cloud sources ('S3', 'GitHub', 'Kaggle'). tl_model() function wraps established implementations 'glmnet', 'randomForest', 'xgboost', 'e1071', 'rpart', 'gbm', 'nnet', 'cluster', 'dbscan', others consistent function signatures tidy tibble output. Results flow unified 'ggplot2'-based visualization optional formatted 'gt' tables via tl_table() family. underlying algorithms unchanged; 'tidylearn' simply makes easier use together. Access raw model objects via $fit slot supervised method, $fit$model unsupervised one. Methods include random forests Breiman (2001) doi:10.1023/:1010933404324 , LASSO regression Tibshirani (1996) doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1996.tb02080.x , elastic net Zou Hastie (2005) doi:10.1111/j.1467-9868.2005.00503.x , support vector machines Cortes Vapnik (1995) doi:10.1007/BF00994018 , gradient boosting Friedman (2001) doi:10.1214/aos/1013203451 .

title: tidylearn: A Unified Tidy Interface to R's Machine Learning Ecosystem — tidylearn-package
text: tidylearn wraps established R machine learning packages behind one consistent interface. main entry points : tl_read Read data files, databases cloud sources tidy tibble. tl_model Fit supported supervised unsupervised method. tl_evaluate Score fitted model. tl_table Render results formatted gt tables. tl_auto_ml Search across methods automatically. Every fitted model keeps underlying package's object $fit slot, package-specific functionality remains available. See vignette("getting-started", package = "tidylearn") walkthrough.

title: Create a tidylearn model — tl_model
text: data data frame containing training data formula formula specifying model. unsupervised methods, use ~ vars NULL; one-sided formula names columns, ~ . - x means every numeric column x. Supervised methods need two-sided formula. method modeling method. Supervised: "linear" (stats::lm), "polynomial" (stats::lm polynomial terms), "logistic" (stats::glm), "tree" (rpart), "forest" (randomForest), "boost" (gbm), "ridge"/"lasso"/"elastic_net" (glmnet), "svm" (e1071), "nn" (nnet), "deep" (keras), "xgboost" (xgboost). method response agree, mismatch error rather meaningless fit: "linear" "polynomial" need numeric response, "logistic" needs exactly two classes, every supervised method takes either. Unsupervised: "pca" (stats::prcomp), "mds" (stats::cmdscale, smacof MASS mds_method), "kmeans" (stats::kmeans), "pam"/"clara" (cluster), "hclust" (stats::hclust), "dbscan" (dbscan). ... Arguments method: see Method arguments section. Anything else passed underlying model function. compute Compute tier fit. One "cpu" (default, existing behaviour), "gpu" (route local CUDA method upstream GPU path – xgboost deep learning today), "auto" (consult tl_compute_advisor pick per call), "cloud" (reserved – yet wired ). "gpu" requested method without upstream GPU path machine without detected GPU, call falls back CPU warning.

code: # \donttest{ if (requireNamespace("xgboost", quietly = TRUE)) {   # The default grid is every combination of the large xgboost grid   # without nrounds -- this many:   default_grid <- tl_default_param_grid("xgboost", size = "large")   prod(lengths(default_grid[names(default_grid) != "nrounds"]))    # Name a smaller one to see it run, and cap nrounds so early stopping   # has less ground to cover. nthread = 2 keeps xgboost from taking   # every core it is offered.   tuned <- tl_tune_xgboost(iris, Species ~ .,     param_grid = list(max_depth = c(2, 4)),     cv_folds = 3, nrounds = 20, verbose = FALSE, nthread = 2)    results <- attr(tuned, "tuning_results")   results$best_params   results$best_iteration    # tuned is an ordinary model, refit on all rows at those settings   predict(tuned, iris[1:5, ]) } #> # A tibble: 5 × 1 #>   .pred  #>   <fct>  #> 1 setosa #> 2 setosa #> 3 setosa #> 4 setosa #> 5 setosa # }

text: New tl_table() dispatcher function — mirrors plot() produces formatted gt tables instead ggplot2 visualisations tl_table_metrics() — styled evaluation metrics table tl_evaluate() tl_table_coefficients() — model coefficients p-values (lm/glm) sorted magnitude (glmnet), conditional highlighting tl_table_confusion() — confusion matrix correct predictions highlighted diagonal tl_table_importance() — ranked feature importance colour gradient tl_table_variance() — PCA variance explained cumulative % coloured tl_table_loadings() — PCA loadings diverging red–blue colour scale tl_table_clusters() — cluster sizes mean feature values kmeans, pam, clara, dbscan, hclust models tl_table_comparison() — side--side multi-model comparison table table functions share consistent gt theme via internal tl_gt_theme() helper gt suggested dependency — functions error install message gt available

title: tidylearn 0.2.0
text: Added “Reporting tidylearn” vignette covering plot table functions

text: First release tidylearn - unified tidy interface R’s machine learning ecosystem

title: tidylearn 0.1.0
text: tl_model() - Single function fit 20+ machine learning models Consistent function signatures across methods Tidy tibble output results Access raw model objects via $fit package-specific functionality

title: tidylearn 0.1.0
text: Linear regression (stats::lm) Polynomial regression (stats::lm poly) Logistic regression (stats::glm) Ridge, LASSO, elastic net (glmnet) Decision trees (rpart) Random forests (randomForest) Gradient boosting (gbm) XGBoost (xgboost) Support vector machines (e1071) Neural networks (nnet) Deep learning (keras, optional)

title: tidylearn 0.1.0
text: Principal Component Analysis (stats::prcomp) Multidimensional Scaling (stats, MASS, smacof) K-means clustering (stats::kmeans) PAM clustering (cluster::pam) CLARA clustering (cluster::clara) Hierarchical clustering (stats::hclust) DBSCAN (dbscan)

title: tidylearn 0.1.0
text: tl_split() - Train/test splitting stratification support tl_prepare_data() - Data preprocessing (scaling, imputation, encoding) tl_evaluate() - Model evaluation multiple metrics tl_auto_ml() - Automated machine learning tl_tune() - Hyperparameter tuning grid random search Unified ggplot2-based visualization functions Integration workflows combining supervised unsupervised learning

title: tidylearn 0.1.0
text: tidylearn wraps established R packages including: stats, glmnet, randomForest, xgboost, gbm, e1071, nnet, rpart, cluster, dbscan, MASS, smacof.
